Who among these was born first?
Stephen Hales (born 1677) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four. Thomas Carlyle (4 December 1795 – 5 February 1881) was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher.
Which of these was founded earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which one below was established earliest?
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Roger Joseph Boscovich is a physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.
What is the atomic number of Unbiquadium?
Unbiquadium, also known as element 124 or eka-uranium, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has placeholder symbol Ubq and atomic number 124.
In what year was David Attenborough born?
David Attenborough: Sir David Frederick Attenborough ( AT-ən-bər-ə; born 8 May 1926) is an English broadcaster, natural historian, and writer.
In what year was Palladium discovered?
Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
In what year was Chromium discovered?
Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.
Mil Mi-28: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. The Mil Mi-28 (NATO reporting name "Havoc") is a Soviet heavy-weight, all-weather, day-night, tandem-seat anti-armour military attack helicopter.
LIGO: United States. The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) is a large-scale physics experiment and observatory designed to detect cosmic gravitational waves.
Who is credited with discovering Tellurium?
Tellurium: Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein. Tellurium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
Who is credited with discovering Einsteinium?
Einsteinium: Albert Ghiorso. Einsteinium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Es and atomic number 99 and is a member of the actinide series and the seventh transuranium element.
Who is credited with discovering Neon?
Neon: William Ramsay. Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
Affecting about 1 in 30,000 newborns, this inherited condition — also called rod monochromacy — brings color blindness, poor acuity, and a curious day-blindness. What is it?
Achromatopsia is a medical syndrome that exhibits symptoms relating to five conditions, most notably monochromacy.
These tropical arachnids are nicknamed 'whip-spiders,' yet they spin no silk and carry no venom — their name actually means 'blunt tail.' Which order are they?
Amblypygi is an order of arachnids also known as whip-spiders or tailless whip-scorpions, not to be confused with whip-scorpions or vinegaroons that belong to the related order Uropygi.
Largely self-taught, this Dutch tradesman-turned-scientist pioneered the use of the microscope and is commonly called the 'Father of Microbiology' — who is he?
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (AHN-tə-nee vahn LAY-vən-hook, -huuk; 24 October 1632 - 26 August 1723) was a Dutch microbiologist and microscopist in the Golden Age of Dutch art, science and technology.

This term describes a statement accepted as self-evidently true, serving as a starting premise for further logical reasoning, derived from a Greek word meaning 'that which is thought worthy' — what is it?
Axiom is a statement that is taken to be true, to serve as a premise or starting point for further reasoning and arguments.
Before TV stardom he was a Boeing mechanical engineer who invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube for 747s, then jumped to sketch comedy on Almost Live! — which science communicator?
Bill Nye (born November 27, 1955) is an American science communicator, television presenter, and former mechanical engineer.
Present in both sexes from the same embryonic tissue, these two prominences on the upper torso permanently enlarge only in human females at puberty, driven by estrogen and growth hormone - name them?
Breast are two prominences located on the upper ventral region of the torso in humans and other primates.
Indigenous to Asia, this genus of flowering plants includes species like sativa, indica, and ruderalis, and is also commonly known as hemp when grown for non-drug purposes — name the genus?
Cannabis is a genus of flowering plants in the family Cannabaceae that is widely accepted as being indigenous to and originating from the continent of Asia.
First flown in 1998, this Chinese-built multirole combat aircraft features a delta wing and canard design and is nicknamed "Vigorous Dragon" — which fighter jet is it?

Chengdu J-10 (pinyin: Jian-Shi), also known as Menglong (pinyin: Menglong; lit. 'Vigorous Dragon'), is a Chinese medium-weight, single-engine, multirole combat aircraft with a delta wing and canard design.
A scale insect native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas that lives on prickly-pear cacti, this parasite is the source of the natural dye carmine — which insect?
Cochineal (-eel, US also, -eel; Dactylopius coccus) is a scale insect in the suborder Sternorrhyncha, from which the natural dye carmine is derived.
This trailing evergreen vine produces a tart berry that starts light green and turns bright red as it ripens on low, creeping stems. What fruit is it?
Cranberry are a group of evergreen dwarf shrubs or trailing vines in the subgenus Oxycoccus of the genus Vaccinium.
With interlocking neck vertebrae that prevent almost any head movement, which genus of prehensile-tailed marsupials is commonly called the large American opossums?
Didelphis is a genus of New World marsupials.

This American theoretical physicist, a professor emeritus at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study, is renowned for foundational contributions to string theory and topological quantum field theory — who is he?
Edward Witten (born August 26, 1951) is an American theoretical physicist known for his contributions to string theory, topological quantum field theory, and various areas of mathematics.
From abortion to animal welfare to business practices, the 'applied' branch of this philosophical study tackles real-world moral problems. What is it?
Ethics is the philosophical study of moral phenomena. Its main branches include normative ethics, applied ethics, and metaethics.
Discovered in 1999 at a Dubna lab, this synthetic superheavy element (symbol Fl, number 114) honors a Russian physicist whose name was transliterated from Cyrillic — which element?
Flerovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fl and atomic number 114.
This branch of medicine has no set starting age, instead guided by a patient's needs and available caregiving, and helps those managing multiple chronic conditions — what is it?
Geriatrics is a medical specialty focused on addressing the unique health needs of older adults.
A retrovirus that gradually dismantles the human immune system, it leads to AIDS and, untreated, shortens life by roughly a decade — what is it?
HIV (HIVs) are two species of Lentivirus (a subgroup of retrovirus) that infect humans.
First unearthed in 1994 in Spain's Gran Dolina cave, this Early Pleistocene human was named 'pioneer man' because it was among the first to settle Western Europe. Which species is it?

Homo antecessor (Latin for 'pioneer man') is an extinct species of archaic human recorded in the Spanish Sierra de Atapuerca, a productive archaeological site, from 1.2 to 0.8 million years ago during the Early Pleistocene.
Aided by Soviet intelligence gathered on the American Manhattan Project, this physicist oversaw the first Soviet nuclear weapon test at Semipalatinsk in 1949 — who is he?
Igor Kurchatov was Soviet nuclear physicist (1903–1960).
This condition causes a yellowish, sometimes greenish, tint to the skin and eyes due to high bilirubin levels, affecting an estimated 80% of babies in their first week of life — what is it called?
Jaundice is a yellowish or, less frequently, greenish pigmentation of the skin and sclera due to high bilirubin levels.
This anesthetic drug induces a trance-like dissociative state while preserving breathing, and its S-enantiomer is now used to treat depression — name it?
Ketamine is a cyclohexanone-derived general anesthetic and NMDA receptor antagonist with analgesic and hallucinogenic properties, used medically for anesthesia, depression, and pain management.
This bacterial blood infection, spread between humans, dogs, and rodents, can range from symptomless to a severe form that turns skin and eyes yellow and shuts down the kidneys — what disease is it?
Leptospirosis is a blood infection caused by bacteria of the genus Leptospira that can infect humans, dogs, rodents, and many other wild and domesticated animals.
This SI unit quantifies the perceived power of visible light emitted by a source, weighted by how sensitive the human eye is to different wavelengths — what is it?
Lumen (unit) (symbol: lm) is the SI unit of luminous flux, which quantifies the perceived power of visible light emitted by a source.

In 1895 this American psychologist completed every requirement for a Harvard Ph.D., only to be refused the degree because of her gender — yet she still invented the paired-associate learning technique. Who was she?
Mary Whiton Calkins (30 March 1863 - 26 February 1930) was an American philosopher and psychologist, whose work informed theory and research of memory, dreams and the self.

Introduced in 1975 and still in production today at two Russian factories, this Soviet-designed helicopter family serves as both a medium twin-turbine transport and, in gunship form, an armed attack aircraft — what's the helicopter?

Mil Mi-17 (NATO reporting name: Hip) is a Soviet-designed Russian military helicopter family introduced in 1975 (Mi-8M), continuing in production as of 2024 at two factories in Russia, in Kazan and Ulan-Ude.
Likened to insulation on an electrical wire, this fatty material sheaths axon segments to speed up the transmission of nerve impulses — what is it called?

Myelin is a lipid-rich material that in most vertebrates surrounds the axons of neurons to insulate them and increase the rate at which electrical impulses (called action potentials) pass along the axon.

Jointly operated by the U.S. Air Force and NASA in the 1960s, this rocket-powered experimental aircraft set speed and altitude records, once reaching Mach 6.7 and crossing into the edge of outer space — name this aircraft?

North American X-15 is a hypersonic rocket-powered aircraft formerly operated by the United States Air Force and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) as part of the X-plane series of experimental aircraft.
Atomic number 8 and a potent oxidizing agent, this element pairs up into a colorless, odorless diatomic gas and tops the list of elements in Earth's crust — what is it?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
This serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity, wrapping most internal organs in a single sheet of mesothelium that also carries their blood vessels and nerves — what's the membrane?
Peritoneum is the serous membrane forming the lining of the abdominal cavity or coelom in amniotes and some invertebrates, such as annelids.
Used in randomized clinical trials to gauge a treatment's true efficacy, this inert pill, injection, or sham surgery has no pharmaceutical effect of its own — what is it?
Placebo (pluh-) is a medicine or treatment intended to appear genuine to its recipient, but which has no pharmaceutical effect.
A byproduct of natural gas processing and petroleum refining, this three-carbon gas becomes liquid under pressure and is a key component of the fuel sold as LPG — what compound is it?
Propane is a three-carbon chain alkane with the molecular formula C3H8.
An Indian industrialist and philanthropist who twice led one of the country's biggest business groups, he descended from its founder and trained as an architect at Cornell. Who was he?
Ratan Tata (28 December 1937 - 9 October 2024) was an Indian industrialist and philanthropist.
The first alkali metal denser than water, this element has a radioactive isotope with a half-life more than three times the age of the universe — which element?
Rubidium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rb and atomic number 37.
This bodily fluid carries reproductive cells along with fructose and enzymes that help them survive their journey toward an egg — name the fluid?
Semen is a bodily fluid that contains spermatozoa from the male gonads of animals.
A white crystalline compound most important industrially as a nitrite salt, and probably best known as a food additive in processed meats. What is it?
Sodium nitrite is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula NaNO2.
This colorless, sweet-smelling liquid with the formula C6H5CH=CH2 is manufactured from benzene as the industrial precursor to a widely used plastic — what compound is it?
Styrene is an organic compound with the chemical formula C6H5CH=CH2.
Also called bush crickets, this insect family in the suborder Ensifera includes over 8,000 mostly nocturnal, leaf-mimicking species — which family?
Tettigoniidae are commonly called katydids (especially in North America) or bush crickets.

This androgenic anabolic steroid, part of the nandrolone group, is marketed in ester forms for veterinary use — commonly given to livestock to boost muscle growth and appetite — what's the steroid called?
Trenbolone is an androgen and anabolic steroid (AAS) of the nandrolone group which itself was never marketed for human use.
This southwestern European viper's bite can be more dangerous than the common adder's — up to 4% of untreated cases are fatal — which species?
Vipera aspis is a viper species found in southwestern Europe.
Known for a rapid side-to-side flight just before landing and living only in colonies, these black-and-yellow social wasps of the genera Vespula and Dolichovespula go by what North American name?
Yellowjacket is the common name in North America for predatory social wasps of the genera Vespula and Dolichovespula.
This class of bony fish accounts for nearly 99% of all living fish species, ranging in size from an 8-millimeter minnow to a giant sunfish weighing 2,700 kilograms — what is it?
Actinopterygii: Class of ray-finned bony fishes.
Its very name comes from the Arabic for 'the kohl,' and chemically it's any compound carrying a hydroxyl group on a saturated carbon — a family that ranges from methanol to cholesterol. What is it?
Alcohol (chemistry): Organic compound with at least one hydroxyl (–OH) group.
Formed when hydrogen atoms in ammonia are swapped out for carbon-based groups, which class of nitrogen-containing organic compounds includes aniline as its simplest aromatic member?
Amine: Chemical compounds and groups containing nitrogen with a lone pair (:N)

Serving as Surveyor of the Queen's Pictures while secretly working as the 'fourth man' of a notorious spy ring, this British art historian wrote a landmark 1967 study of the painter Nicolas Poussin — who is he?
Anthony Blunt: British art historian and Soviet spy (1907–1983)
Painting, sculpture, and architecture are its three classical visual branches, yet nobody can agree on a single definition for it; what cultural pursuit of creative and imaginative talent is this?
Art: Creative work to evoke aesthetic response.
This slender projection of a nerve cell typically carries electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands — what is it called?
Axon: Long projection on a neuron that conducts signals to other neurons.
A colorless, sweet-smelling liquid hiding in petroleum, this ring-shaped hydrocarbon helps give gasoline its distinctive aroma — what is it?
Despite being just 12 to 20 cm long, this small marine creature's vivid markings flash brighter when it feels threatened, and its bite delivers a neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Blue-ringed octopus: Four species of mollusk.

Unique among mammals, human females are the only ones to permanently develop this secondary sex organ at puberty rather than just during pregnancy, and it later produces milk via the mammary gland — which body part?
Breast: Part of the female primate torso that has mammary glands.
The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust and a reactive alkaline earth metal, this element's name comes from the Latin word for 'lime' obtained by heating limestone — what is it?
Calcium: Chemical element with atomic number 20 (Ca)
Extracted from the cochineal insect, this bright-red pigment is also known by the food-additive code E120 — what is it called?
Carmine: Pigment, aluminium salt of carminic acid.
Around 20 millimetres long with a shimmering structural-green shell and a coppery underside, this beetle is identified by its isosceles-triangle scutellum — which species?
Cetonia aurata: Species of beetle. The scutellum is the small V-shaped area between the wing cases; it may show several small, irregular, white lines and marks.
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Used to treat gout, familial Mediterranean fever, and pericarditis, this medication has such a narrow therapeutic index that its injectable form was pulled from the US market in 2008. What is it?
Colchicine: Medication mainly used to treat gout. The American College of Rheumatology recommends colchicine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or steroids in the treatment of gout.
Home to crows, ravens, magpies, and jays, this bird family boasts a brain-to-body ratio rivaling great apes, and one of its members even passed the mirror self-recognition test — what family is this?

A Scottish biologist, classicist and mathematician who pioneered theoretical biology, he's remembered for his 1917 book On Growth and Form, which opened the way to explaining how patterns and body structures take shape — who was he?
D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson: Scottish biologist, mathematician, and classics scholar.
Defined as having at least three loose or watery bowel movements in a single day, this condition is most often caused by an intestinal infection from contaminated food or water — what is it?

Diarrhea: Loose or liquid bowel movements. Diarrhea (American English), also spelled diarrhoea (British English), is the condition of having at least three loose, liquid, or watery bowel movements in a day.
Element 105 sparked a long Cold War naming dispute, claimed first by a Soviet institute in 1968 and then by Berkeley in 1970 before being settled in 1993 — which synthetic element?
Dubnium: Chemical element with atomic number 105 (Db)
The second-largest member of the deer family, this animal is also called "wapiti," a Shawnee and Cree word meaning "white rump" for the pale fur it flashes to signal alarm — what animal is it?
Elk: Species of deer. The word "elk" originally referred to the European variety of the moose, Alces alces, but was transferred to Cervus canadensis by North American colonists.

In 2019 this French-American MIT economist shared the Nobel with her husband and Michael Kremer for an experimental approach to fighting global poverty, rooted in the randomized trials of her J-PAL lab — who is she?
This front-of-the-head body part houses most sense organs — eyes, nose, and mouth — and its damage or scarring can profoundly affect a person's sense of identity. What is it?
Face: Front of a head. The face is the front of the head in humans and many other animals that features most of the sense organs including the eyes, nose and mouth.
This normal, occasionally embarrassing bodily process brings intestinal gas to the rectum, pressurizes it with muscle contractions, and releases it through the anus — what is it?
Flatulence: Bodily function of expelling intestinal gas from the anus.

After dropping out of Harvard to help build early versions of Windows at Microsoft, this developer co-founded a studio that made Half-Life and later launched a digital storefront called Steam — who is he?
Known only from teeth and four jawbones, this extinct genus of giant ape roamed China for nearly two million years and is now thought to be a close relative of the orangutan — what is it?
Gigantopithecus: Extinct genus of primate. The species may have been sexually dimorphic, with males much bigger than females.
The largest and most widespread member of its rosy-pink family, this wading bird ranges from Sub-Saharan Africa to the Mediterranean and Central Asia — which species?
Caused by mutations in the ABCA12 gene, this severe genetic skin disorder covers newborns in thick, cracked plates resembling armor — what is it?
Harlequin-type ichthyosis: Genetic skin disease. Harlequin-type ichthyosis is a genetic disorder that results in thickened skin over nearly the entire body at birth.

This American philosopher co-created an algorithm for the Boolean satisfiability problem and helped prove Hilbert's tenth problem unsolvable — all while reshaping the philosophy of mind and language. Who was he?
Hilary Putnam: American mathematician and philosopher (1926–2016)

Made of one oxygen and one hydrogen atom bonded together with a negative charge, this ion is the active base in the sodium compound used to produce millions of tons of industrial chemicals yearly. What ion is it?
Expressed with symbols like < and >, this relation shows that one quantity is less than or greater than another, rather than equal — what's it called?
Inequality (mathematics): Mathematical relation making a non-equal comparison.
An English mathematician who shaped matrix and invariant theory, he founded the American Journal of Mathematics while leading the field at Johns Hopkins — who was he?
This British-American designer ran industrial design at Apple alongside Steve Jobs, then founded the creative collective LoveFrom working with Ferrari and OpenAI — who is he?
The largest joint in the human body, it's a modified hinge that links the thigh to the lower leg via two separate joints — what is it?
Knee: Leg joint in primates. The knee is a modified hinge joint, which permits flexion and extension as well as slight internal and external rotation.

This small wild feline of South and Southeast Asia sports dark spots on a tawny coat and two stripes running from its eyes to its ears, and can live as high as 4,474 meters in the Himalayas — what is it?
Leopard cat: Small wild cat species. The leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis) is a small wild cat with dark spots on the tawny-coloured body and limbs.

This American stealth strike fighter comes in three flavors — conventional, short-takeoff/vertical-landing, and carrier-based — and with 883 in service is the world's fourth-most-numerous military aircraft. What is it?

Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II: American stealth multirole fighter aircraft. The Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II is an American family of single-seat, single-engine, supersonic stealth strike fighters.
Element number 12 is so eager to ignite that, once lit, it burns with a brilliant-white light — this lightweight alkaline-earth metal, less dense than aluminium, is what?
Magnesium: Chemical element with atomic number 12 (Mg)

This field studies abstract things like numbers, shapes, sets and probabilities, using logical proof to establish truths it calls theorems — and its branches include algebra, geometry and number theory. What is it?
Mathematics: Field of knowledge. Mathematics is a field of knowledge concerned with abstract concepts such as numbers, geometric shapes, sets, functions, and probabilities.
Sold under the brand name Dolophine, this synthetic opioid is used to manage chronic pain and treat opioid use disorder by relieving cravings and withdrawal. What is it?
Methadone: Opioid analgesic and maintenance therapy.

Also called 'selective sound sensitivity syndrome,' this disorder causes specific sounds to trigger strong negative emotional and physiological reactions, though it isn't yet listed in the DSM-5-TR — what is it called?
Misophonia: Disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds.

Made of contractile proteins called actin and myosin, this soft tissue exists in three vertebrate forms — skeletal, cardiac, and smooth — and forms during a developmental process called myogenesis — what is it?
Muscle: Important Biological tissue that allows movement.
Roughly how many Earth years does Neptune take to complete one orbit of the Sun?
Neptune orbits once every 164.8 years at about 30 astronomical units. It has completed only one full orbit since its discovery in 1846.
Built from a nitrogen-containing base, a five-carbon sugar, and a phosphate group, these molecules are the monomer building blocks of DNA and RNA — what are they called?
Nucleotide: Biological molecules constituting nucleic acids.
Nicknamed 'brittle bone disease,' this genetic disorder causes fragile bones and blue-tinted eye whites, usually stemming from faulty type I collagen — what is it?
Osteogenesis imperfecta: Group of genetic disorders resulting in fragile bones.

Also called the blue passionflower, this South American vine climbs via tendrils to 10 metres, bears fragrant blue-white blooms with a fringed coronal filament, and produces an edible but not particularly tasty orange fruit — which plant is it?
Passiflora caerulea: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.
Usually caused by a virus but sometimes by strep bacteria, this inflammation of the back of the throat brings on a sore throat, fever, and sometimes a hoarse voice — what is it called?
Pharyngitis: Inflammation of the back of the throat. Pharyngitis is a type of upper respiratory tract infection.
Used in randomized clinical trials as a genuine-looking but pharmacologically inert stand-in — like a sugar pill or saline shot — what's this sham treatment called?
Placebo: Substance or treatment of no therapeutic value.
This rare genetic disorder linked to chromosome 15 leaves affected children constantly hungry, often leading to obesity, alongside a narrow forehead and small hands and feet — what is it?
Prader–Willi syndrome: Genetic disorder involving an imprinted genomic region.
This term covers the laws, regulations, and government actions that address issues from education to healthcare to transportation — what is it?
Public policy: Government proposals, principles and actions.
One of the oldest groups of eukaryotic seaweed, this phylum boasts over 7,000 species — mostly marine, though about 5% live in freshwater habitats. What group is it?
Red algae: Division of plant life.

Also called black locust or false acacia, this deciduous legume-family tree is native to just a few small pockets of the United States but has been planted so widely it's now considered invasive elsewhere — which tree?
Robinia pseudoacacia: Species of tree native to North America.
Containing the potent compound salvinorin A, this plant used by Mazatec shamans for spiritual healing sparked a US media panic around 2007 after being shared in online videos — which plant?
Salvia divinorum: Species of plant. The leaves contain the potent compound salvinorin A and can induce a dissociative state and hallucinations.
Ejaculated through the urethra and containing fructose plus enzymes that help sperm survive their journey to fertilize an egg, this bodily fluid is also collected for animal breeding. What is it?
Semen: Reproductive biofluid of male or hermaphroditic animals.

A parasomnia in which wakefulness and deep non-REM sleep occur in different brain regions at once, this condition can produce anything from bathroom trips to attempts at cooking or even driving — what is it?
Sleepwalking: Sleeping phenomenon combined with wakefulness.

Synthesized by Aristotle and taken as fact for two millennia, this superseded theory held that maggots could arise straight from dead flesh, until Louis Pasteur helped discredit it — what was it called?
Spontaneous generation: Theory of life arising from non-living matter.
Codenamed 'Flanker' by NATO, this Soviet twin-engine fighter entered service in 1985 as an air-superiority answer to the F-14 and F-15 — what is it?
Sukhoi Su-27: Soviet 4th generation fighter aircraft.
This Japanese immunologist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with James P. Allison for identifying the PD-1 protein — who is he?
Tasuku Honjo: Japanese immunologist and Nobel laureate (born 1942)
In tetrapods this body region between the neck and abdomen houses the heart, lungs, and thymus gland, while in insects and crustaceans it forms one of three main body segments — what is it called?
Thorax: Frontal part of an animal's body, between its head and abdomen.
Usually caused by a new genetic mutation rather than inherited, which disorder produces deformities of the ears, eyes, cheekbones, and chin but typically leaves intelligence normal?
Treacher Collins syndrome: Human genetic disorder. The degree to which a person is affected may vary from mild to severe.
Roughly 20 to 30 centimeters long in adults, this smooth-muscle tube carries urine from each kidney down to the bladder — what is it called?
Ureter: Tubes used in the urinary system in most animals.
Known as the 'true foxes,' animals in this genus are smaller and bushier-tailed than any wolf or jackal, with a signature dark triangular mask between the eyes — which genus?
Vulpes: Genus of true foxes. The members of this genus are colloquially referred to as true foxes, meaning they form a proper clade.
Made up of eight carpal bones and home to the carpal tunnel and the anatomical snuff box, this joint connects the hand to the forearm — which body part?
Wrist: Part of the arm between the lower arm and the hand.
The symbol for carbon is C. Carbon is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
What is the chemical symbol for hafnium?
The symbol for hafnium is Hf. Hafnium is a chemical element; it has symbol Hf and atomic number 72.

In what year was Mel Brooks born?
Mel Brooks: Melvin James Brooks (né Kaminsky; born June 28, 1926) is an American actor, filmmaker, comedian, songwriter, and playwright.
In what year was Gisele Bündchen born?
Gisele Bündchen: Gisele Caroline Bündchen (Brazilian Portuguese: [ʒiˈzɛli ˈbĩtʃẽ], German: [ˈbʏntçn̩]; born 20 July 1980) is a Brazilian supermodel and activist.
In what year was Elliot Page born?

Laurence Fishburne: Laurence John Fishburne III (born July 30, 1961) is an American actor.
In what year was Stanley Tucci born?
Stanley Tucci: Stanley Tucci Jr. ( TOO-chee, Italian: [ˈtuttʃi]; born November 11, 1960) is an American actor.
In what year was Melanie Lynskey born?
Melanie Lynskey: Melanie Jayne Lynskey ( LIN-skee; born 16 May 1977) is a New Zealand actress.
In what year was Henry Cavill born?
Henry Cavill: Henry William Dalgliesh Cavill ( KAV-əl; born 5 May 1983) is a British actor.

Clint Eastwood: Clinton Eastwood Jr. (born May 31, 1930) is a retired American actor, filmmaker, and musician.
